A spatial molecular atlas of the relapsing–remitting EAE cycle

RRMAP2 spinal-cord Xenium · RELAPSE-REMITTING cohort · 33 animals, ~894k cells, 5101-gene panel · animal-level pseudobulk. Two coupled axes of disease variation: a temporal relapse cycle and a spatial L→T→C gradient.

Headline. Disease is organized along two coupled axes. In time, the relapse cycle splits genes into an acute reversible program (flares each relapse, resets) and an irreversible cumulative program (ratchets up). In space, the same disease program is concentrated in lumbar cord and declines rostrally toward cervical. Space and time encode the same biology — the spatial epicenter is the temporally most-advanced state.

What this is — in plain language

The disease. These mice have EAE (experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis), the standard animal model of multiple sclerosis (MS): the immune system attacks the myelin insulation around nerve fibres in the spinal cord, causing weakness and paralysis. In the relapsing–remitting form studied here (the most common form of MS), an animal goes through attacks (relapses, the ‘peaks’) followed by partial recovery (remissions); we also compare a chronic form that steadily worsens without recovering.

The data. Xenium is imaging-based spatial transcriptomics — it measures ~5,000 genes in every individual cell while keeping that cell’s physical position in the tissue. Here that is ~894,000 cells across spinal-cord sections from 33 relapsing-remitting mice (plus a chronic comparison group). Each mouse is sampled once, at a single point in its disease, and given a clinical score (0 = healthy, 3+ = paralysis) for how sick it is at that moment.

What we did, and the one idea to take away. We mapped how gene activity and cell types change as the disease waxes and wanes — over time (the relapse cycle) and through space (along the cord). One theme recurs: two kinds of change. An acute, reversible response that flares during an attack and then resets, and an irreversible, cumulative build-up of damage that never fully clears. Almost everything we measured tracks ‘how sick the animal is right now’ — with one exception that matters: the accumulated damage keeps growing with disease duration, even between two equally-sick animals.

How to read this. Green boxes are the main findings, blue boxes are the key quantified results, orange boxes are caveats and limits. Gene names appear in monospace (e.g. Hal). Every number is reproducible from the script named in its section. ‘ρ’ (rho) is a correlation from −1 to +1; ‘q’ / ‘p’ are significance values (smaller = stronger evidence).

Study design & the relapse cycle

Each mouse is one snapshot at one disease stage, so the ‘cycle’ below is reconstructed by lining up many mice caught at different points — not a film of one animal.

Terminal cross-sectional: one stage per animal (n shown), so the cycle is a cross-animal reconstruction, not a within-animal time course. Region, by contrast, is a within-animal axis (32/33 animals span all three levels) — fully de-confounded from severity, batch and strain, and the better-powered backbone.

Read the axis carefully. The raw region gradient is dominated by Hox positional-identity genes (posterior Hoxa9/b9/a10/c8 high in lumbar, anterior Hoxa5/b5 high in cervical) — anatomy, not disease. The disease component runs the same way: inflammation, complement and demyelination peak in lumbar; neurons and intact myelin increase toward cervical.

Lesion architecture — radial organization

Segmenting lesions and profiling against signed distance-to-edge (scripts/lesion_radial.py, 570 lesions) recovers a textbook concentric structure de novo: inflammatory-myeloid + demyelinated core → lymphocyte + complement margin at the edge → reactive-astrocyte rim just outside → spared myelin parenchyma.

Myeloid states — recruitment → activation → resolution

The inflammatory-myeloid compartment is three distinct states that organize both in time and in the lesion's radial space: c18 recruitment/antigen-presenting/IFN (Ccr2, Plac8, Ciita, Cd74, Cxcl10), most peripheral (−11µm, the margin where cells enter); c5 acute glycolytic/M2 (Arg1, Chil3, Acod1, Hal), deepest in the core (−25µm) and the clean acute oscillator; c3 repair/resident-like (Mrc1, Igf1, C6), the persistent baseline. The c5↔c3 swing drives the cycle — c5 38%→9% peak→remission (p=0.009), c3 44%→70% (p=0.014). c18 is +12.6µm more peripheral than c5 (p=8e-7); astrocytes sit +44µm outside the core. So recruitment is peripheral, activation is in the core; resolution is an in-place temporal hand-off, not a migration (ordering inferred from a cross-sectional snapshot).

Lesion signaling wiring (spatial ligand-receptor)

Neighborhood-enrichment + ligand-receptor analysis on a per-section graph (the precomputed global graph had 14.6% spurious cross-section edges; rebuilt block-diagonal). Adjacency matches the radial model: T cells embedded in the myeloid core (z≈+100–146), B/plasma a tight follicle-like aggregate (z+567) adjacent to T cells, and reactive astrocytes avoid the core (z −28 to −125 — the rim is spatially segregated). Signaling: complement dominates (C3→C3ar1/C5ar1, with reactive astrocytes the top C3 source — notable as C1q is off-panel); astrocyte→microglia Csf1/Il34→Csf1r maintenance; recruitment Ccl2→Ccr2, Cxcl10→Cxcr3; lymphoid Cxcl13→Cxcr5; costim Cd80/86→Ctla4/Cd28.

This is the signaling structure of a severity-driven state — wiring, not a signal beyond severity.

Space × time — does the spatial gradient recapitulate the cycle?

Time and space could be two unrelated stories. They turn out to be the same story told twice — the lower cord is, molecularly, the most disease-advanced region.

Yes — and the sign is the punchline. The per-gene region slope (L→T→C) and the relapse-cycle trend correlate -0.57 (Spearman over 1206 moving genes; -0.59 genome-wide). It is negative: the program that rises over disease time is the same program concentrated in lumbar space. Space and time are two readouts of one disease trajectory, with lumbar = the most advanced state and progression running caudal→rostral.

Cross-model conservation — the program is strain-invariant

Is this specific to one mouse strain, or general EAE biology? A second, independent model (a different strain and disease course) says the core program is the same.

The atlas is built on the RR (SJL/PLP) cohort. The independent chronic cohort (B6/MOG — different strain, antigen and course) has its own severity trajectory (3587 genes q<0.05, batch-robust). Correlating the two models' within-model slopes cancels the strain offset:

Chronic severity trend vs RR relapse-cycle trend: Spearman +0.78 (5101 genes, p≈0). The same disease program runs in both models — a strain-invariant EAE signature: complement/DAM up (C6, Gpnmb, C4b, Abca1, Ctss, C3ar1, Csf1r), cholesterol-biosynthesis/myelin down (Msmo1, Idi1, Hmgcr, Lss, Mal, Plp1, Mog).
Unique to chronic, but blocked. A severity × disease-duration grid (day-16 vs day-30 sacrifice at matched score) could separate active inflammation from chronic accrual — but here the day axis is perfectly confounded with run_date, so it needs matched-batch sampling. Key wet-lab follow-up.

Cellular composition

The 25 leiden_1 niches label to: oligo/myelin ×5, neuron ×4, vascular/endo ×4, infl-myeloid ×3, astrocyte ×2, microglia ×2, OPC ×2, T/NK ×1, ependymal ×1, Bcell/plasma ×1.

Same clinical score, different molecular state — the accrual axis

Two mice can look equally sick on the clinical scale yet be in different molecular states — because the score sees current activity but not the damage piled up from earlier attacks.

The clinical score reads current disease activity (the reversible acute program) but is largely blind to accumulated, irreversible damage, which grows with disease history. So the same score can be a molecularly different state depending on how many relapses preceded it.

Strain-clean test (within RR): PEAK1 vs PEAK3 at near-identical score (2.75 vs 2.65). The cumulative program rises (z -0.97 → +0.13, p=0.016) — Gpnmb 1.9→2.7→3.2, Fcrls 0.2→0.8→1.0 — while the acute program does not accrue (Hal flat 1.32/1.10/1.19; p=0.19). Reaching the same score at a later relapse means more accumulated damage on a comparable acute flare.

Chronic PEAK1 is strain-confounded. Its absolute position mixes disease history AND genetic background (B6/MOG vs SJL/PLP), so it can't be cleanly compared to the RR peaks. One striking confounded difference: Hal — the headline RR acute marker — is essentially absent at the chronic peak (0.03 vs ~1.2–1.3 in RR), the one gene that cleared FDR in the severity×model interaction; relapse-biology vs strain can't be resolved here. Small n (4–6) throughout — descriptive.

Duration axis — accrual tracks actual time, not just cycle number

day_of_sacrifice (~11–49 days post-induction) is real disease duration. Within RR the relapse cycle decouples it from severity (collinearity only +0.14), so a partial Spearman | severity isolates the time effect, strain-matched:

Cumulative program vs day | severity: partial ρ = +0.69 (p≈0; Fmod +0.81, Igf2 +0.73, Fcrls +0.65; 844 genes accrue with time after severity adjustment). The acute program does not — it wanes (ρ -0.59; Hal −0.05, Arg1 −0.58). At matched severity, later disease = more accumulated damage on a weaker acute flare.
Chronic corroborates your late-timepoint intuition (cumulative vs day | severity = +0.72), and its day-16 vs day-30 matched-severity pairs are the discrete version (day-30 higher in Gpnmb, Cd68, Fmod at equal grade). But chronic's time axis is confounded with run_date (day16/day30 are different batches) and more collinear with severity (+0.58), so it corroborates rather than independently confirms.

Beyond severity — tested to exhaustion, consistently null

Could the rich molecular data tell us something the simple clinical score cannot? We looked hard, at every level of detail — and the honest answer is no.

Is anything separable from current disease severity (trajectory direction, lesion architecture)? Tested and null at every layer: bulk expression, 10 spatial niches, 25 cell types, composition, whole-lesion geometry (888 lesions; count/size/confluence track severity but 0/22 peak-vs-rem and 0/22 region tests survive residualization), and — newest — lesion internal organization (core-rim polarization of myeloid/astrocyte/complement programs, residualized on severity + lesion size: null, peak-vs-rem p=0.25–0.88, region p=0.41–0.90). Severity is the organizing axis; the state is a faithful readout of it down to the radial architecture of individual lesions. Separating 'direction of travel' or 'lesion age' from severity would need longitudinal sampling, not a different analysis.

Vignette — Hal and its cell of origin

A spotlight on the single most reproducible gene in the dataset — what it is, which cell carries it, and why we read it cautiously.

The single most reproducible disease-associated gene. A clean acute oscillator (resets each remission), ~10.7× concentrated in leiden_1 cluster 5 — an inflammatory antigen-presenting myeloid state (Arg1, Chil3, Cd14, Cd74, Gpnmb; homeostatic microglia low). So Hal marks infiltrating/activated myeloid cells, not resident microglia or neutrophils.

The histidine-catabolism reading (bridge to 'histidine↓ in MS') is a hypothesis only — a dedicated review found it weak. Here Hal is best presented as a robust marker of the acute myeloid relapse state. Detail: docs/hal-histidine-deep-research.md.

Scope & honest limits

Cross-sectional in time (no within-animal trajectory; no causal claims); small per-stage n (2–5 animals). The spatial axis is within-animal and well powered, but its raw form is dominated by Hox positional identity — disease signal must be read against that backdrop. Disease activity (severity) is the organizing variable by design; there is no separately identifiable 'direction of travel' beyond severity (tested null in bulk, niches, cell types and composition — see relapse_phase_feasibility.html).
